lesson_title: Day 7 Daily Quiz: Review of Day 6 (the Bitcoin trace lab: heuristics, false positives and confidence)

lectures.title: Bitcoin trace lab: following a ransom to the first service

questions.question_stem: A ransom trace shows one transaction spending two ransom addresses as inputs. What do you write for the link?
questions.correct_answer: Co-spend: one wallet holds both addresses; it fails if the transaction is a CoinJoin; Moderate.
incorrect_answers: Co-spend: one wallet holds both addresses; it cannot fail, because inputs need one key; High.
Change clue: the second input is the change; it fails if the wallet is a CoinJoin; Moderate.
Co-spend: the two addresses belong to the payer and the payee; it fails on a reuse; Low.
questions.explanation: A trace entry names the heuristic, the known false positive and a confidence on the course scale. Co-spend assumes one wallet signed every input, and a CoinJoin is where that fails. Here the outputs are two unlike amounts, not an equal-output shape, so Moderate stands.

questions.question_stem: A transaction pays 0.5 BTC to a P2SH address and 1.512279 BTC to a P2WPKH address, like the input. Why does the change call stop at Moderate?
questions.correct_answer: Script type and round amount both come from one transaction, so they count as one kind of evidence.
incorrect_answers: The two clues contradict each other, so they cancel out and leave only a guess at the change.
Moderate is the lowest word on the scale, so any call about a change output has to use that one word.
A round amount marks the change, so the clue is certain but the script type adds some doubt.
questions.explanation: High needs two or more independent kinds of evidence with no known failure. Type and amount of outputs of the same transaction are one kind, and a wallet that pays a round sum to a P2WPKH address would defeat both. Moderate is the ceiling here.
questions.lesson_block: Why clues from one transaction stop at Moderate

questions.question_stem: Three hops each pay a round amount to a non-P2WPKH address and roll an un-round remainder to a new P2WPKH address. What is the pattern, and how do you record the peels?
questions.correct_answer: A peel chain; record each peel as a lead with its next transaction, as an exchange's withdrawals look the same.
incorrect_answers: A CoinJoin; record each peel as the attacker's wallet, because steps that look alike show only one owner.
A peel chain; record each peel as the attacker's wallet, because the repeat of the pattern settles exactly who owns it.
A batch payout; record the remainder as a lead, because one input can feed many different payees in one go.
questions.explanation: A peel chain peels a payment off and rolls the remainder forward. The pattern is regular, but an exchange's withdrawals look alike, and a regular pattern is one kind of evidence. So the peels are leads, each followed to its next transaction, at Moderate.

questions.question_stem: A transaction has 12 inputs, 11 of which received once from different earlier transactions, and one output of 2.5178 BTC. Is it a sweep or a CoinJoin?
questions.correct_answer: A sweep: one output of one amount is not a CoinJoin's equal-output shape; a service gathering deposits fits.
incorrect_answers: A CoinJoin: twelve inputs from separate sources are what a mixing round looks like here to an analyst.
A CoinJoin: a service that gathers coins from separate sources pays them out as equal outputs, so it mixes them.
A sweep: the single output belongs to the thief, so the 11 other inputs are the thief's own deposits.
questions.explanation: A CoinJoin has several equal outputs, so that its coins cannot be matched one to one. One output of one amount cannot hide who owns what; co-spend then says one wallet holds all 12 inputs. The chain does not say which service. The lab rates it Moderate.

questions.question_stem: The trail ends at a transaction with 1 input and 14 outputs, 13 to different addresses. What do you report?
questions.correct_answer: A batch payout by a service, so the trail has reached it; the chain cannot name it, and the call is Low until labelled.
incorrect_answers: A CoinJoin round, so the trail stops here; all 14 outputs are equally likely to be the attacker's, with no way to choose.
A peel chain with 13 peels, so the trail goes on; the 14th output is the change, and so it holds all of the ransom that is left.
A batch payout by the attacker, so the 13 recipients are accomplices; the call is High on the shape of the payout alone.
questions.explanation: One input paying many addresses is payment batching, which exchanges and other services use. The recipients are other people's addresses, so the trace ends. A business or a mixer batches too, and without a source label the pattern alone is Low.
